title: Types of Machine Learning: Supervised, Unsupervised, Self-Supervised, and Reinforcement Learning
learningObjectives: Distinguish four learning setups by their feedback signal.
Identify the data and objective each setup needs.
Choose a learning setup for a product problem.

mentalModel.text: The key question is what signal teaches the system. Supervised learning gets target answers. Unsupervised learning searches for structure without target labels. Self-supervised learning derives targets from the data itself. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards tied to actions and outcomes.

blocks.text: The learning setup is determined by feedback, not model size or whether data is text. A language model can use self-supervised pretraining and later be fine-tuned with supervised examples.

The key question is what signal teaches the system. Supervised learning gets target answers. Unsupervised learning searches for structure without target labels. Self-supervised learning derives targets from the data itself. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards tied to actions and outcomes.

concepts.title: Technical deep dive and worked example

blocks.text: Supervised training compares predictions with known targets. Unsupervised methods optimize structure objectives such as clustering. Self-supervised training constructs targets automatically, such as the next token. RL connects states, actions, rewards, and future states; feedback can be delayed and actions can change future observations.

blocks.problem: You have 50,000 support tickets: some have assigned queues, some have only raw text, and you want to optimize which reply to show first.
reasoning: Use trustworthy queue labels for supervised classification.
Use clustering to explore themes when labels are absent; validate group meaning with humans.
Use next-token prediction as a self-supervised objective on raw text.
Consider RL only if actions affect future states and a meaningful long-term reward can be measured safely.
blocks.outcome: Name the learning signal and intended outcome before choosing an algorithm.

blocks.title: Reinforcement-learning loop

blocks.text: Read the diagram clockwise: observe the current state → the policy chooses an action → the environment changes → the agent receives a reward and next state → the loop repeats. This is a conceptual diagram, not runnable Python. Unlike a single supervised example, the action can change which future states and rewards are observed.
Expected output: This is a conceptual loop: observe state, choose action, receive reward and next state, then update the policy/value estimate.

Supervised quality depends on labels. Unsupervised groups need interpretation and stability checks. Self-supervision scales with raw data but may not match the business task. RL adds reward-design, exploration, and safety complexity.
Production check: For a recommendation system, clicks alone may not represent long-term user value. Define the reward, safety constraints, and offline baseline before considering online exploration.

blocks.title: Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: Calling clusters ground-truth classes; assuming self-supervised means no objective; using RL just because a product has a feedback button.

blocks.text: 1. Problem — The dataset has raw examples, partial labels, and perhaps feedback. The available learning signal constrains what can be learned.
2. Choice — Supervised uses target labels; unsupervised finds structure; self-supervised derives targets from inputs; reinforcement learning uses rewards for actions.

3. Mechanism — Supervised training compares predictions to targets. Self-supervised next-token training shifts text to make the next token the target. RL observes state, chooses an action, then receives reward and next state.

4. Trade-offs and scale — Labeling 10,000 examples at an assumed 30 seconds per label takes about 300,000 seconds, or 83 hours, before review and quality control. Self-supervision can use raw text without that per-example labeling, but its objective may not match the business task. RL also needs safe interaction/reward data.
5. Avoid — Calling clusters ground-truth classes, saying self-supervised has no objective, and adopting RL only because feedback exists.
6. Interview probes — What is the signal? Is the target known? Do actions affect later states? Can a simpler supervised baseline meet the goal?

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Engineering rule of thumb
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Choose the learning paradigm based on the available feedback and the outcome the system must optimize.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.text: Supervised quality depends on labels. Unsupervised groups need interpretation and stability checks. Self-supervision scales with raw data but may not match the business task. RL adds reward-design, exploration, and safety complexity.

revisionSheet.text: Supervised = labeled targets; unsupervised = discover structure; self-supervised = derive targets from input; RL = action/reward feedback.
Next-token prediction is self-supervised; it does not by itself teach a business-specific label taxonomy.
RL is useful when sequential actions affect future outcomes and the reward represents the goal.

questions.prompt: Which dataset best supports supervised training?
questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses examples paired with target answers.

questions.prompt: What is a typical unsupervised-learning goal?

options.text: Predict a known label for every row
Discover groups or structure in unlabeled data

questions.explanation: Clustering can discover structure without known class labels.

questions.prompt: A team has billions of unlabeled text tokens and wants to pretrain a language model. Which training signal can be constructed directly from the text?

options.text: Predict the next token from preceding tokens
Require a human to label every token as helpful or harmful
Cluster documents and assume cluster IDs are factual answers
Reward an environment action without defining a state

questions.explanation: The next token provides a target for the preceding context. This makes training self-supervised, although later adaptation may still be needed for the product task.

questions.prompt: A robot chooses actions that affect its future position and receives delayed rewards for reaching a goal. Which learning setup best matches this problem?
questions.explanation: The action changes future states and success is expressed through reward over a sequence, which is the defining RL setup. A simpler approach may still work, but the feedback structure is sequential.

questions.prompt: Unsupervised learning has no objective function.
questions.explanation: Unsupervised methods still optimize objectives; they simply do not rely on explicit target labels in the same way.

questions.prompt: Any app with thumbs-up/down feedback automatically requires RL.
questions.explanation: Feedback can support evaluation, supervised preference data, or analytics; RL is only one possible use.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A retailer has purchase histories but no segment labels and wants to explore groups.
strongAnswerPoints: Start with unsupervised clustering or embeddings plus clustering.
Prevent IDs from dominating distance and inspect feature scaling.
Check stability and interpretability; treat clusters as hypotheses.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would explore unsupervised grouping, test stability under resampling, and inspect useful behavioral differences. Business usefulness must be validated separately.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A feed team wants to use RL to maximize clicks. What risks do you raise?
strongAnswerPoints: Check whether clicks reflect long-term user value.
Define state, actions, delayed reward, and safety constraints.
Compare with supervised ranking and use guarded experiments if RL is justified.
pitfalls: Optimizing clicks without measuring user harm
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would challenge the reward first: clicks can reward sensational content without improving outcomes. I would define a broader objective and compare with a simpler ranking baseline.
